profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the Strategy Research lead and the Content Marketing manager at a fintech company preparing a cross-functional launch package for a thought-leadership article on DeFi market structure. The company plans to publish a technical blog post and a companion executive brief based on a research note arguing that all AMMs are CFMMs, that every DeFi market has an invariant, and that arbitrage-freeness is equivalent to having an increasing invariant. The meeting context is that research has finished the core draft and marketing needs to coordinate the handoff for web publication, sales enablement, and social promotion. The agenda is to align on what version of the research note is being handed over, what 'final' deliverables marketing will receive by Thursday, what content is included in the executive brief versus the technical post, and how review and approval will happen. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the Thursday handoff, review path, and ownership of the publication assets, while leaving several subtle second-order assumptions misaligned.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: DeFi market structure, quantitative research translation, technical writing
members.background: Nina leads a small internal research team at a digital-assets analytics firm and regularly converts dense academic ideas into practitioner-facing explainers for clients and the company blog.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the precision of the theorem statements, avoid legal or reputational risk from overclaiming, and minimize last-minute revision cycles because her team is already committed to the next report.
hidden_assumptions: When she says the paper is on the 'final draft,' she means the research argument, theorem statements, and examples are frozen, but copyediting and packaging changes can still happen around them.
The 'executive brief' naturally excludes the appendix-style examples on fees, liquidity operations, and multi-pool coordination unless someone explicitly asks for them.
A 'reviewed' launch package means marketing has done formatting and clarity edits, while research only needs to re-check technical claims in the near-final layout.
The working source for the piece is the Google Doc labeled v12, because that is where research comments and equation fixes are tracked.

members.name: Lucas Meyer
members.expertise: B2B content operations, launch coordination, executive messaging
members.background: Lucas manages the publication pipeline for white papers, blog posts, sales one-pagers, and social assets at a fintech firm and is responsible for moving expert material into launch-ready collateral across channels.
members.private_state: He wants a clean, low-friction handoff that lets his team produce web, social, and sales assets quickly, and he is trying to avoid reopening content once design and scheduling have started.
hidden_assumptions: When he hears 'final draft,' he assumes the document is publication-stable and that only cosmetic edits remain before publishing.
The 'executive brief' should include the practical examples on fees, liquidity operations, and multiple pools because those are what sales and clients will latch onto.
A 'reviewed' package means all stakeholders, especially research, have substantively approved the exact files that will be published and reused downstream.
The handoff source of truth is the Notion page linked in the campaign tracker, because that is what design, web, and social teams pull from.
Once assets move into layout on Thursday, research changes should be limited to obvious factual corrections, not structural or scope changes.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to handing over the 'final draft' on Thursday
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the technical substance is finalized in the research draft, but headline wording, examples included in derivative assets, and presentation framing may still be adjusted around that core.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the deliverable is effectively publication-ready, with no meaningful content changes expected after Thursday beyond copy polish or formatting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In content operations, 'final draft' is a routine phrase that sounds fully aligned; both expect professionalism from the other side and do not think to unpack whether 'final' refers to technical substance or publication readiness.

misalignment_points.topic: Which source document is the current master
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss using 'the latest version' and 'the main doc' for the handoff
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the Google Doc v12 that contains the latest theorem wording and equation corrections from research.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the Notion campaign page version that his team duplicated into their publication workflow after the previous review.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams regularly say 'latest version' and 'main doc' because each function has its own operational hub; since titles are similar and both systems are actively updated, the mismatch feels too mundane to question.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the executive brief
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the executive brief will cover the 'practical examples' and the 'core implications'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the executive brief will stay tightly scoped to the main equivalences and maybe one lightweight example, while operational edge cases like fees, liquidity operations, and coordinated multi-pool examples remain in the full technical post.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the executive brief includes a concise treatment of those practical examples because they are necessary to make the message commercially useful and easier for nontechnical readers to anchor on.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe they are endorsing accessibility and practical relevance, but neither sees the inclusion boundary as a major decision worth formalizing during a coordination check-in.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as reviewed before publish
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the package should be 'reviewed' before it goes live
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks review is satisfied if research verifies technical accuracy in the near-final blog post and brief, even if social snippets, email copy, and derivative summaries are only loosely checked.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks review is satisfied only when research has effectively signed off on the exact package of downstream assets that will reuse the claims, including social cards and sales-facing summary text.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'reviewed' usually signals diligence rather than a precise acceptance threshold; because both are cooperative and deadline-oriented, they assume the other shares their implicit standard for sufficiency.

turns.inner_thought: We should be fine for Thursday as long as nobody treats this like an invitation to reopen the argument. The theorem statements, examples in the research note, and core framing are set on our side. I can still tolerate packaging edits around the edges, but I do not want a new revision cycle once my team moves to the next report.
turns.utterance: From the research side, we're on track to hand over the final draft on Thursday. I mainly wanted to confirm the downstream handoff path for the DeFi invariants piece so there aren't any surprises once your team picks it up.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If Thursday is truly the final draft, we can put design, web, and social into motion without risking churn. I need the latest version in the main doc early enough that the campaign workflow can start that afternoon, because once layout begins I really don't want substantive changes sneaking back in.
turns.utterance: That timing works on my end. If we can have the latest version ready early enough, web, design, and social can all start from the main doc that afternoon and keep the launch schedule intact.

turns.inner_thought: The Google Doc v12 already has the settled theorem language and the equation fixes from this morning, so the research substance is stable. If marketing is working from that, great. I just need them to preserve the technical wording where it matters and not pull from an older copy.
turns.utterance: That should be workable. The latest version already has the theorem language settled, and we wrapped a few equation and wording cleanups in the draft this morning, so the core substance is in good shape.

turns.inner_thought: The brief has to be usable by sales and client-facing teams, not just a compressed abstract. If it covers the core implications and practical examples, especially the ones people can relate to operationally, it'll actually travel across channels.
turns.utterance: Great. On the packaging side, I want to make sure the executive brief really distills the core implications and practical examples so sales can pick it up right away with nontechnical prospects.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, practical is fine, but I still want the brief disciplined. It should center the main equivalences and not turn into a mini appendix. The examples on fees, liquidity operations, and multi-pool coordination belong in the full technical post unless someone explicitly decides otherwise, and I'd rather not create extra legal or reputational exposure by oversimplifying them.
turns.utterance: I agree with keeping it practical. The brief can focus on the main equivalences and the core implications, while the fuller practical examples can live in the technical post where we have the room to handle them carefully.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds aligned enough. I still need the brief to include a concise treatment of the practical examples people will actually remember, otherwise it won't help sales. A few lines on fees, liquidity operations, and multiple pools should be easy to carry over without making it feel too technical.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I do think a couple of lines on the practical examples in the brief will help anchor the message commercially, but the overall shape you're describing works.

turns.inner_thought: We need to keep the approval loop tight. Research can sanity-check the near-final blog and brief for technical accuracy, but I do not have bandwidth for a sprawling asset-by-asset approval process. If marketing handles formatting and clarity, a quick reviewed pass before publish should be enough.
turns.utterance: On process, once marketing has the draft, research can do a quick reviewed pass on the near-final materials before publish. That should let us catch anything important without slowing the handoff.

turns.inner_thought: I need that to mean the whole package is substantively approved, not just the longform pieces. If research reviews the exact language before launch, then I can safely cascade it into the brief, web copy, email, and social without reopening things later.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. I want the full package reviewed before it goes live so the same language can safely flow into the brief, web page, email copy, and social assets.

turns.inner_thought: As long as they preserve the technical wording from Google Doc v12, I can live with the rest. They should route edits against the current document so we don't end up reconciling parallel copies or accidentally reintroducing older phrasing in the theorem section.
turns.utterance: That should be fine as long as the technical wording from the latest draft stays intact. If your team can route edits against the current document, we'll be able to review cleanly and keep things moving.

turns.inner_thought: We'll keep moving from the Notion page in the campaign tracker since that's what every downstream team uses. As long as the main doc there reflects the final draft, we won't lose Thursday to coordination overhead. I just need research not to send late structural changes after layout starts.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. My team will work from the main doc in the campaign tracker and keep the final draft moving through the pipeline so we don't lose Thursday layout time.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I can send the Thursday handoff and be done from the research side except for a final technical check. I assume we're aligned that the brief stays centered on the core implications, with the practical examples handled at the right level, and that review is a quick near-final pass rather than a prolonged signoff cycle.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll send over the final draft Thursday morning, and I'm glad we're aligned on the brief, the practical examples, and the review flow.

turns.inner_thought: Great. Thursday gives us enough runway if the latest version in the main doc is truly publication-stable and reviewed across the package. Then design, web, and sales assets can all launch off the same source without last-minute content churn.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. We'll plan around the Thursday handoff, a quick review, and launch prep from the latest version so the whole team stays on schedule.
